content:
This is the first installation of a two-part opinion piece by Edward Cavanagh that commences a cautionary tale: understanding what it was that motivated China to develop a relationship with Australian wines and wineries provides a few clues about why the industry needs to be more careful in the future.

I have been struck recently by articles that have been published in different formats on the crisis faced by an export-dependent Australian wine industry that uncritically repeat some of the same tropes that were rehearsed during similar periods of malaise in the decades that followed 1927, 1973 and 2004. Like our current period, those were also moments in time during which overseas market evaporation led to domestic market reconfiguration and viticultural scaling back.

Separately, I have also been reflecting on an interchange I had on LinkedIn with Ashley Ratcliffe, a well-known and outspoken grower from the Riverland, who is always a voice worth listening to.

In a throwaway and perhaps slightly unserious comment, Ratcliffe wrote that the disappearance of ‘China’, as an export market, was a ‘sucker punch […] which no one could have predicted’.

The issue I have with this presumption is that it dooms the Australian wine industry to the fate of repeating past mistakes.

For decades, industry levies have been used to pay for marketing initiatives. Ideally, this should involve as much budget allocation towards generic promotion as it does towards the critical assessment of the potential risks that might arise within particular overseas markets on the basis of demographic, political, financial and geopolitical analysis.

In the sequel to this article, I intend to explain how and why it was that China disappeared as a major trading partner – and what that meant for the Australian wine industry.

It falls to this article here, however, to explain where the Chinese market came from in the first place, and along the way, to identify a number of factors that should have been acknowledged, at the time, when it did so.

 

The strategic republic

After a decade of strategically pegging its own currency to a cheap exchange rate deliberately to become a more powerfully export-oriented country – addicting Western consumerist nations to cheap manufactured imports in the process – China began to tinker very carefully with its currency policy in the mid-2000s.

By allowing the yuan to appreciate in value after 2005, the People’s Republic of China slowly attained an appetite for imports.

And that included wine.

In 2006, China overtook the USA and the UK, erstwhile Australia’s most important overseas markets, as the leading importer of Australian wines by value. And this figure climbed steadily every year, such that by 2013/2014, Australia was sending as much wine to China as it was sending to the UK and the USA put together. And this was in spite of the imposition of a 14% tariff on Australian wine at the Chinese end! Coincidentally, it was also around this time, that is, between the second quarter of 2013 and first quarter of 2016, that the Australian currency began a gradual slide in value, after nearly three years of more-or-less parity with the USD, to finish up still healthy but closer to where it probably more naturally belonged at this time, which was around the US$0.70-0.80 mark.

“Out of nowhere, China turned up in Australia.”

Wine provides a rather small part of a much bigger story about the ways in which closer economic relations between Australia and China were developed over this period.

And this story is partly to do with Australia’s fortune in escaping from the GFC mostly unscathed and with a reputation for stability as a trading partner despite its high exchange rates, which conduced to a rise in domestic discretionary spending in Australia.

But this story is also partly to do with an unprecedentedly large public spending programme rolled out by the People’s Republic of China, which corresponded with a huge surge in demand for Australian iron ore and concentrates, coal, and minerals, which conduced to a change in domestic spending habits within Chinese society too.

 

Open sesame

Starting in the Howard years, and continuing through the Rudd-Gillard period, Australia entered into trade talks with China. After 21 rounds of negotiations, a free trade agreement finally came together towards the start of 2015. The China Australia Free Trade Agreement (ChAFTA) was signed and ratified by Australian Trade and Investment Minister, Andrew Robb, and the PRC’s Commerce Minister, Gao Hucheng, on 17 June 2015, and it was celebrated by Treasurer Joe Hockey for its creation of ‘a two-way investment flow’.

Owing to a number of reasons that were way outside of Australia’s control or influence in the months that followed this ratification – including a brief and unplanned devaluation of the yuan and a crash on the Shanghai stock exchange – the investment flow that was eventually inspired by this new arrangement turned out to be strikingly one-sided. Chinese investors of all shapes and sizes were spooked and began to look for safe havens. With its high-value real estate sector, established industries, and an overall economy that seemed insulated from the knock-on effects of quantitative easing that were seen in the USA and the Eurozone, Australia seemed to offer the place for Chinese investment capital after the ratification ChAFTA that few trade experts could have expected in the earlier stages of the negotiations.

Under the 2015 agreement, China agreed to remove entirely the tariff on wine by 2019, which effectively they did through tapering: it fell to 11.2% in December 2015, then to 8.4% in 2016, then to 5.6% in 2017, then to 2.8% in 2018, and finally it was removed altogether in January 2019. If the value of Australian wine exports to China had become considerable even before this reduction of the tariff rate, then it reached extraordinary highs in 2019. By that year, Australia became the leading wine exporter in China by value, overtaking France to take the top spot, and dwarfing every other competing nation.

There were other sweeteners, both within this deal and in legislative changes adjacent to it, for the PRC that are worth considering in the context of the wine industry.

The agreement was accompanied by a liberalisation of visa laws for Chinese citizens in Australia. The process for applying for student visas was significantly simplified, and a new working holiday visa for Chinese citizens was offered to a maximum of 5,000 per year. And now a pathway to permanent residency for any approved investment greater than $1.5 million – the significant investment visa, which was first established in 2012 – was increasingly available to new Chinese investors, subject only to the approval of those investments by the Foreign Investment Review Board.

“And before long Australia bridled the entire wine industry onto the dragon.”

The Foreign Acquisitions and Takeovers Act 1975 was then amended in December 2015 to provide for an even higher threshold for screening foreign investments by the Foreign Investment Review Board. This raised the cap imposed on Chinese investors from $252 million to $1.427 billion, although investments in vineyards were subject to a ceiling of $55 million, since it remained the policy of the government to prevent too much agricultural land from passing into foreign ownership. Still, the extent to which winery production, logistics, and sales operations fell within the scope of ‘agribusiness’ so-defined would remain ambiguous, and this undoubtedly handed quite a bit of discretion to the Foreign Investment Review Board.

It is probably not an irrelevance to point out that one of Joe Hockey’s appointments to the board in December 2013 was Patrick Secker, who had been the Member for Barker (which included the Barossa, the Riverland, and the whole of the Limestone Coast, and therefore the vast majority of South Australian viticultural country), from 1998 all the way up to his deselection in 2012. Widely considered at the time to be an example of ‘a job for the boys’, the installation of Secker into the Foreign Investment Review Board for a five-year term in December 2013, over a period which saw a number of applications for Chinese wine industry investment, probably had at least some bearing on the prioritisation of certain investments over others, given his intimate knowledge of the industry and significant and well-publicised links to the major winery businesses in Australia. But this is mere speculation, and hardly is it an accusation.

Anyhow, one of the major roles of the Foreign Investment Review Board was to screen the applications of Chinese state-owned enterprises with greater diligence than private Chinese investors. But in practice the line between these two was probably very blurry, given the way that the PRC both found itself heavily involved in the mechanisms through which loan capital found its way to investors, and indeed actively encouraged foreign investment in this period.

There is a suggestion that has occasionally been made to me and in certain media reports, which I have no way or intention of proving in this article, that certain Chinese investors and syndicates were gently goaded in these years – whether by former politicians, Wine Australia board members, diplomats, businesspeople, academics, local mayors, state premiers, federal treasurers, or members of the Foreign Investment Review Board – into investing in certain parts of the Australian sector, like the wine industry, in order to make their applications for more ‘sensitive sectors’ likelier to succeed. If this is even remotely true, then there is at least some reason to suspect that a few of the almost random and out-of-nowhere counter-cyclical investments into the grape and wine sector by hulking Chinese investors in these years were not motivated by any serious desire to make these acquisitions profitable, but were simply seen as part of the collateral expense involved in doing more coordinated, lucrative and strategic business deals in Australia.

Whatever the motivations behind their acquisitions, it remains undoubtedly the case that a small but significant flurry of takeovers and acquisitions by Chinese investors of mostly small Australian winery businesses corresponded with a gigantic surge in exports of wine to China at the time. And this activity together propped up the wine industry for a few important years. Many of these 50 or so Chinese-owned winery businesses even became profitable as a result, no doubt, of their knowledge about, and their connections within, the all-important home market that these new Chinese owners brought with them.

“As it had done several times before, the wine industry placed all of its bets upon an export market, and then expected trustingly that the windfalls would just last forever.”

 

A market appears

Out of nowhere, China turned up in Australia.

But nobody important troubled themselves to ask why.

And before long Australia bridled the entire wine industry onto the dragon.

As it had done several times before, the wine industry placed all of its bets upon an export market, and then expected trustingly that the windfalls would just last forever.

One effect of this unexpected boost for the industry was the reversal of what had been a noticeable trend between 2008 and 2014 in the direction of vineyard removals in Australia.

Australia needed fewer vines, and that was a forecast that vineyard operators were only just beginning to clue into before all of this happened. After the national area under vine reached an incredible 166,197ha in 2007/08, this figure thereafter began to drop slightly with every year.

The market had delivered its message, and the sector had finally started to react.

Until China.

In 2018, the downward trend stopped. This left the area under vine steady at around 146,128ha (which, incidentally, was basically what it had been in 2002, and represented probably – on the surface of it – around 40,000 or 50,000ha more than the country still probably needed). And this area would stablise and hover around this mark for a few years more, instead of continuing along its natural downward trajectory.

All of this was largely if not entirely due to a new sense of optimism about exports principally to China.

How this played out for the Australian grape and wine sector will be deferred to the sequel, but the understatement that it does not turn out too well will suffice to round this article off here.

Read part 2 in the October 2026 issue of Grapegrower & Winemaker.

This article was originally published in the September issue of the Australian & New Zealand Grapegrower & Winemaker. To find out more about our monthly magazine, or to subscribe, click here!

title: Second generation takes the reins at Mortimers Wines in Orange
summary:
More than 30 years after husband-and-wife duo Peter and Julie founded Mortimers Wines, son Daniel and his wife Tasley have now taken ownership of the winery, becoming the second generation to lead the family business. For Daniel Mortimer, the path to ownership of Mortimers Wines began in childhood, working in the vineyard on the family property in Orange alongside his parents and his four brothers. Daniel returned to Orange in 2019 following a 10-year NRL career, which included a Grand Final appearance with the Parramatta Eels in 2009 and a Premiership with the Sydney Roosters in 2013. “Long before rugby league, I was growing up amongst the vines on our family property just north of Orange. It’s always been a big part of who I am, and I’m incredibly excited to carry the family legacy forward,” he said.

The post Second generation takes the reins at Mortimers Wines in Orange appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
Daniel and his wife Tasley have taken ownership of Mortimers Wines. Image credit Monique Lovick

More than 30 years after husband-and-wife duo Peter and Julie founded Mortimers Wines, son Daniel and his wife Tasley have now taken ownership of the winery, becoming the second generation to lead the family business.

For Daniel Mortimer, the path to ownership of Mortimers Wines began in childhood, working in the vineyard on the family property in Orange alongside his parents and his four brothers.

Daniel returned to Orange in 2019 following a 10-year NRL career, which included a Grand Final appearance with the Parramatta Eels in 2009 and a Premiership with the Sydney Roosters in 2013.

“Long before rugby league, I was growing up amongst the vines on our family property just north of Orange. It’s always been a big part of who I am, and I’m incredibly excited to carry the family legacy forward,” he said.

Daniel has spent the last six years working alongside Peter as general manager, learning the business inside and out. During that time, the winery explained that he has immersed himself in the broader wine industry, being selected for Wine Australia’s Future Leaders program in 2025 and currently serving as vice president of the Orange Region Vignerons Association.

Tasley (Taz) steps into ownership alongside husband Daniel, bringing her own strengths to the business with experience in marketing and events.

“We want to focus our energy on two things: making quality wines that reflect the best of the Orange Wine Region and providing a wonderful space for guests to enjoy them. Orange is such a beautiful town, and its popularity continues to grow, particularly among Sydneysiders looking for a weekend away,” she said.

For Peter and Julie, the handover brings their original hopes for the property full circle.

“There are so many wonderful memories of raising our five sons on the property. It has given us more than we could have asked for. To see Dan and Taz take ownership and keep Mortimers in the family is a very proud moment,” they shared.

The family marked the transition in July with an ‘End of an Era’ members’ dinner, providing an opportunity to reflect on and celebrate what Peter and Julie have built, while welcoming Daniel and Tasley into the next chapter.

“Dad won three premierships with the Canterbury Bulldogs in the ’80s, but there’s no doubt Mortimers Wines is his greatest accomplishment,” said Daniel.

“We’re incredibly proud of what Mum and Dad built…our job now is to respect that history, keep what makes Mortimers special and put our own mark on where it goes next.”

The Mortimers cellar door is housed in the restored former March Public School, established in 1866.

title: Mandoon Estate takes Perth Royal wine show top honour as WA claims 14 trophies
summary:

Mandoon Estate, located at Caversham in the Swan Valley region, claimed the coveted Best Wine of the Show, following four days of rigorous blind judging at Claremont Showground in Perth, from 7–10 September. The prestigious competition brought together wine from regions all over Australia, showcasing the quality and diversity of wine across 59 classes spanning Chardonnay, Chenin Blanc and Riesling to Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, sparkling, fortified wines and more. Mandoon Estate’s 2025 Cabernet Sauvignon emerged as the standout of the competition, not only taking home the top honour for Best Wine of the Show, but Best Red Wine, Best Cabernet Sauvignon, and The John Jens Perpetual Trophy for Best Western Australian Wine of Show. Mandoon Estate also claimed the Best Sparkling Wine trophy for their 2018 Reserve Sparkling, securing five trophies in total.

content:
Image: Ryan Sudano, senior winemaker at Mandoon Estate (left), and Brendan Bate from HLB Mann Judd. Photo: Dan MacBride, courtesy Perth Royal Food Awards

Mandoon Estate’s 2025 Cabernet Sauvignon has been named Best Wine of the Show at the 2026 Perth Royal Food Awards – Wine, with Western Australian producers taking 14 of the 21 trophies.

Mandoon Estate, located at Caversham in the Swan Valley region, claimed the coveted Best Wine of the Show, following four days of rigorous blind judging at Claremont Showground in Perth, from 7–10 September.

The prestigious competition brought together wine from regions all over Australia, showcasing the quality and diversity of wine across 59 classes spanning Chardonnay, Chenin Blanc and Riesling to Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, sparkling, fortified wines and more.

Mandoon Estate’s 2025 Cabernet Sauvignon emerged as the standout of the competition, not only taking home the top honour for Best Wine of the Show, but Best Red Wine, Best Cabernet Sauvignon, and The John Jens Perpetual Trophy for Best Western Australian Wine of Show. Mandoon Estate also claimed the Best Sparkling Wine trophy for their 2018 Reserve Sparkling, securing five trophies in total.

Western Australian producers delivered another exceptional performance, securing 14 of the 21 trophies awarded, with winning wines spanning the Swan Valley, Perth Hills, Margaret River, Geographe and Great Southern wine regions.

WA’s diverse geography and climate play an important role in the character of its wines, with growing conditions varying significantly across the State’s wine regions. From the maritime influence of Margaret River to the cooler conditions of the Great Southern and the warm climate and long winemaking history of the Swan Valley, that diversity allows different varietals, styles and regional expressions to thrive.

Among this year’s major winners, Castle Rock Estate’s (Albany, WA) A&W Riesling (vintages 2011, 2018 and 2024) were awarded the trophy for Best Wines of Provenance – Best Red or White Varietal, Jacob’s Creek (Rowland Flat, SA) took home the Best Rosé trophy for their 2026 Le Petit Rosé, and Morris Wines (Yenda, NSW) received the trophy for Best Fortified Wine for their Old Premium Rare Muscat.

A new chapter was also added to the competition in 2026 with the presentation of the inaugural trophy for Best Australian Chenin Blanc won by Jadran Wines (Orange Grove, WA) for their 2026 Reserve Chenin Blanc, which also won Best White Wine and Best Dry White Varietal.

Introduced to celebrate Western Australia’s longstanding connection with Chenin Blanc while recognising excellence in the variety nationally, the new trophy for Best Australian Chenin Blanc draws on both the grape’s history and one of winemaking’s oldest traditions.

Chenin Blanc first arrived in Western Australia via South Africa in 1829, with the first vines planted by Thomas Waters in the Swan Valley the following year. Almost two centuries later, the variety continues to flourish in one of the state’s oldest and most significant wine regions.

Rather than a conventional trophy, Jadran Wines received a handcrafted 55-litre Tava ceramic amphora, a contemporary take on the ancient winemaking vessel used for thousands of years to ferment and mature wine.

 

 

Leading this year’s judging panel was Chief Judge Steve Flamsteed, one of Australia’s most respected winemakers and recently crowned 2027 Halliday Wine Companion Winemaker of the Year.

Over four days, wines were assessed by panels of respected industry experts, with judges having no knowledge of the identity of the wines before awards were determined.

Entries were evaluated on colour and clarity, bouquet and palate characteristics using the internationally recognised 100-point scoring system, with a score of 95 or above required to earn Gold. The top Gold Medal wines were then reassessed to determine Champion winners.

In total, judges awarded 89 Gold Medals, 136 Silver Medals and 288 Bronze Medals, alongside 21 Champion trophies.

Chief Judge Steve Flamsteed said Australia’s wine show system played an important role not only in recognising excellence, but in strengthening the industry and wine community.

“The Australian wine show system is arguably the best in the world. I’ve travelled a few other countries and seen what they do for wine shows, and there’s nothing that compares to the rigour and the diversity of the people actually judging the wines that we see in Australia.

“One of the really important things is that it brings wine judges, winemakers, wine communicators and the broader industry together in one room, and you get this opportunity for mentoring, discussion and sharing ideas. That networking and mentoring is incredibly important to building the culture of Australian wine.”

Royal Agricultural Society of Western Australia CEO Robyn Sermon said the Perth Royal Food Awards celebrated not only exceptional wines, but the people, regions and agricultural industries behind them.

“Western Australia has an extraordinary reputation for premium wine, and that begins in the vineyard, with our growers, our diverse regions and the quality of the produce that ultimately ends up in the glass.

“One of the great strengths of Western Australian wine is the diversity of the places it comes from. Different climates, landscapes and growing conditions allow producers to create wines with a distinctive sense of place.

“For more than 180 years, wine judging has formed part of the Royal Agricultural Society of WA’s story. While the industry has transformed enormously in that time, our purpose remains the same, to recognise quality, encourage excellence and celebrate the people behind our produce,” Sermon said.

 

Winners | Special Awards

  • Trophy for Best Wine of the Show | Mandoon Estate (Caversham, WA) – 2025 Cabernet Sauvignon
  • Trophy for Best Rosé | Jacob’s Creek (Rowland Flat, SA) – 2026 Le Petit Rosé
  • Trophy for Best Sparkling Wine | Mandoon Estate (Caversham, WA) – 2018 Reserve Sparkling
  • The John Jens Perpetual Trophy for Best Western Australian Wine of Show | Mandoon Estate (Caversham, WA) – 2025 Cabernet Sauvignon
  • Trophy for Best White Wine | Jadran Wines (Orange Grove, WA) – 2026 Reserve Chenin Blanc
  • Trophy for Best Red Wine | Mandoon Estate (Caversham, WA) – 2025 Cabernet Sauvignon
  • Trophy for Wines of Provenance Best Red or White Varietal | Castle Rock Estate (Albany, WA) – 2011, 2018, 2024 A&W Riesling
  • Trophy for Best Fortified Wine | Morris Wines (Yenda, NSW) – Old Premium Rare Muscat
  • Trophy for Best Australian Chenin Blanc | Jadran Wines (Orange Grove, WA) – 2026 Reserve Chenin Blanc

Winners | White Trophies

  • Trophy for Best Chardonnay | Evans & Tate (Margaret River, WA) – 2023 Redbrook Reserve Chardonnay
  • Trophy for Best Riesling | Jim Barry Wines (Clare, SA) – 2026 Watervale Riesling
  • Trophy for Best Semillon | Tyrrell’s Wines (Pokolbin, NSW) – 2026 HVD Semillon
  • Trophy for Best Sauvignon Blanc | Pinnacle Drinks | Once & Well – Frankie’s Garden Margaret River Sauvignon Blanc (Margaret River, WA)
  • Trophy for Best White Varietal | Jadran Wines (Orange Grove, WA) – 2026 Reserve Chenin Blanc
  • Trophy for Best Semillon Sauvignon Blanc / Sauvignon Blanc Semillon | Devil’s Lair (Forest Grove, WA) – 2026 Margaret River Hidden Cave Sauvignon Blanc
  • Trophy for Best Sweet White Wine | De Bortoli Wines – 2022 Noble One (Bilbul, NSW)

Winners | Red Trophies

  • Trophy for Best Cabernet Sauvignon | Mandoon Estate (Caversham, WA) – 2025 Cabernet Sauvignon
  • Trophy for Best Shiraz | Smallwater Estate Shiraz (Donnybrook, WA) – 2025 Smallwater Estate Shiraz
  • Trophy for Best Pinot Noir | Tasmanian Vintners (Rosny Park, Tas) – 2025 Sandy Bay Estate Pinot Noir
  • Trophy for Best Red Varietal | Serafino Wines (McLaren Vale, SA) – 2025 Serafino Reserve Granache
  • Trophy for Best Red Wine (Blends) | Oakover Vineyards (Middle Swan, WA) – 2025 Estate Grenache, Shiraz, Mourvedre

title: Ballandean Estate wins Queensland Winery of the Year again
summary:
Ballandean Estate has won Queensland Winery of the Year for the third consecutive year, while head winemaker Boxi Zhen was named Winemaker of the Year at the 2026 Queensland Wine Awards. The double honour marks another chapter in a remarkable story for Queensland's oldest family owned and operated winery, nestled in the heart of the Granite Belt region. The estate claimed 39 points and 16 medals from 16 entries, medalling every single wine it submitted. The achievement is the first time in Ballandean Estate's history that every entry has been recognised. Across a competition that drew 141 wines from 18 producers across 15 classes, the result placed the estate just one point ahead of neighbouring Golden Grove Estate. This margin reflects the strength of both wineries and the quality of the terroir, and speaks to the warm, enduring rivalry between the Puglisi and Costanzo families, two of the Granite Belt's most celebrated winemaking names.

content:
(L to R) Robyn Puglisi-Henderson, Angelo Puglis and Boxi Zhen. Image supplied

Ballandean Estate has won Queensland Winery of the Year for the third consecutive year, while head winemaker Boxi Zhen was named Winemaker of the Year at the 2026 Queensland Wine Awards. The double honour marks another chapter in a remarkable story for Queensland’s oldest family owned and operated winery, nestled in the heart of the Granite Belt region.

The estate claimed 39 points and 16 medals from 16 entries, medalling every single wine it submitted. The achievement is the first time in Ballandean Estate’s history that every entry has been recognised. Across a competition that drew 141 wines from 18 producers across 15 classes, the result placed the estate just one point ahead of neighbouring Golden Grove Estate. This margin reflects the strength of both wineries and the quality of the terroir, and speaks to the warm, enduring rivalry between the Puglisi and Costanzo families, two of the Granite Belt’s most celebrated winemaking names.

At the heart of the result were two standout performances from the estate’s Saperavi. The Ballandean Estate Saperavi 2025 took Top Gold at 96 points in the Open Reds class, while the Fortified Saperavi 2025 also claimed Gold at 95 points in the Fortified Wines class.

Chair of Judges Andrew Santarossa praised the wine and the variety, saying: “A joy to judge. Fantastic bracket of Saperavi. Well done”.

Saperavi, a rare red variety with deep colour and bold flavour, has become a signature for the estate. The estate’s 2023 Saperavi, named Wild Card Wine of the Year in the recent James Halliday 2027 awards, adds further weight to the Granite Belt’s reputation for producing wines of genuine national distinction.

Robyn Puglisi-Henderson, one of the estate’s fourth-generation custodians, reflects on what the achievement means for the family,

“Mum and Dad planted our first Shiraz vines in 1968, and by 1975 we were winning national gold medals at the Royal Queensland Show in Brisbane. To now stand here, more than fifty years on, with medals for every single wine we entered and our third consecutive Winery of the Year award, it is a challenge to find the words to do this justice.

“Moments like this remind us of just how extraordinary their vision was. Angelo and Mary Puglisi set out prove that the high altitude and freezing winters of the Granite Belt could produce premium cool climate wines, and to establish wine tourism in the area, while actively rebelling against two heavy forces: government policy and the entire Australian wine establishment.

“This is their legacy. Every bottle we pour carries faith in their vision, pioneering spirit, and resilience in the face of flood, fire and hail.”

Boxi Zhen earned Winemaker of the Year for his work across Ballandean Estate and Riversands Wines, amassing five gold medals across his winemaking portfolio.

The recognition builds on a career that has quickly become one of Queensland’s most compelling winemaking stories. Boxi Zhen joined Ballandean Estate in late 2022, bringing with him a Master of Viticulture and Oenology from the University of Adelaide, a degree in Food Science, and vintages across Napa Valley, China, and South Australia. His minimal-intervention approach, favouring wild yeasts and a deep respect for Granite Belt terroir, earned him the Emerging Queensland Winemaker of the Year title at the Royal Queensland Wine Awards in 2024, along with gold medals and trophies at the Royal Queensland Wine Awards and the Australian Mediterranean Varieties Wine Show, and 95-point ratings from James Halliday. With this year’s Winemaker of the Year, Zhen has stepped from emerging talent to Queensland’s leading expression in the cellar.

title: AI fire detection expands for use near SA wine regions
summary:
A new AI-powered bushfire detection camera has been activated at Mount Crawford in the northern Mount Lofty Ranges, an area adjoining the Adelaide Hills and Barossa wine regions, ahead of the 2026-27 fire danger season. It’s the first time this technology has operated in a peri-urban area in South Australia after demonstrating its value as a fire detection tool across the Limestone Coast over the past three fire danger seasons. The new fire detection camera comes as part of a partnership between the SA Government, ForestrySA and emergency fire services including the South Australian Country Fire Service, with the AI-powered technology coming online for the first time in a particularly fire-prone section of the southern Barossa and northern Adelaide Hills.

The post AI fire detection expands for use near SA wine regions appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
A fire tower in the Limestone Coast region. Image supplied

A new AI-powered bushfire detection camera has been activated at Mount Crawford in the northern Mount Lofty Ranges, an area adjoining the Adelaide Hills and Barossa wine regions, ahead of the 2026-27 fire danger season.

It’s the first time this technology has operated in a peri-urban area in South Australia after demonstrating its value as a fire detection tool across the Limestone Coast over the past three fire danger seasons.

The new fire detection camera comes as part of a partnership between the SA Government, ForestrySA and emergency fire services including the South Australian Country Fire Service, with the AI-powered technology coming online for the first time in a particularly fire-prone section of the southern Barossa and northern Adelaide Hills.

The camera is located on an upgraded fire tower within ForestrySA’s Mount Crawford estate. It captures ultra-high-definition panoramic vision that is fed into a system combining AI, satellite technology and human verification to identify potential smoke and fire activity.

The system, delivered by bushfire detection and intelligence provider Pano AI, provides real-time alerts and intelligence on fire location, behaviour and proximity to people, assets and firefighting resources, supporting more informed decision-making by emergency services and land managers.

It builds on the implementation of eight AI-powered bushfire detection cameras across the Limestone Coast forestry region, funded by the state government and managed by the Green Triangle Fire Alliance.

The Limestone Coast camera network detected nearly 90 unplanned fires over the past three fire danger seasons.

The newly operational AI camera unit at Mount Crawford Forest provides the SA Government with an opportunity to assess how the technology performs in a more complex peri-urban landscape, where plantations, native vegetation, farms, businesses, infrastructure and residential communities are closely interconnected.

SA Minister for Primary Industries and Regional Development Clare Scriven said the Mount Crawford location provided an opportunity to test the technology in that environment.

“Early detection is one of the most effective tools we have to reduce the impact of bushfires, and this new AI-powered camera will help emergency services identify and respond to threats sooner,” she said.

“Mount Crawford sits at the intersection of forests, primary industries and communities, making it an ideal location to assess how this technology performs in a peri-urban environment.

“This investment builds on the proven success of the Limestone Coast AI fire detection camera network and reflects our commitment to embracing innovation that strengthens resilience, protects livelihoods and keeps South Australians safe.”

ForestrySA chief executive Nathan Paine said the technology would add another layer to existing fire detection and response capabilities.

“We have a responsibility to protect our forests and help safeguard neighbouring communities, businesses, farms, and the environment,” he said.

“The activation of this camera at Mount Crawford strengthens our ability to detect potential fire activity earlier and share critical information with emergency services, supporting faster and more informed responses.

“This technology complements, rather than replaces, existing detection systems and firefighting resources. It adds another layer of capability to the strong network already provided by emergency services, including the Mount Lofty Fire Tower and other fire detection and response assets.

content:
Chief winemaker Virginia Wilcock of Vasse Felix, which has reached a Three Merit classification for its Tom Cullity Cabernet Sauvignon Malbec. Image supplied

The Real Review has announced the 2026 annual update to its Wine Classification of Australia.

A total of 664 Australian wines are now classified across ‘One’, ‘Two’ and ‘Three Merit’ tiers, “establishing the definitive benchmark of consistency for sommeliers, wine buyers, distributors and producers”.

The Real Review Wine Classification is calculated solely on a wine’s review performance over time. To qualify, a wine must have been reviewed blind by The Real Review’s tasting panel over a period of at least ten years.

The Merit classifications are as follows

  • Three Merit classification – “Reserved for iconic wines representing fewer than 0.5% of all wines on the market, achieving consistent top vintage scores of 98 points or higher”.
  • Two Merit classification – “Awarded to wines regularly reaching top vintage scores of 96 points or higher”.
  • One Merit classification – “Recognises outstanding wines with top vintages consistently scoring 95 points or higher”.

Once classified, a wine retains its tier for a minimum of four years. The Real Review said this rule “provides trade buyers and wineries with commercial stability against vintage variation while allowing superior performers to move upward during each annual update”.

“The Real Review Wine Classification is an essential tool for the wine trade because it assesses wines beyond marketing or auction pricing and focuses purely on provenance and quality in the glass over a decade or more,” said Huon Hooke, principal wine writer at The Real Review.

“For trade buyers, it provides confidence when building a wine list or collection of Australian icon wines for retail sales. For Australian wineries, achieving a Merit classification serves as an independent mark of distinction that validates years of vineyard focus and winemaking consistency.

“With each new year, new trends emerge and producers are inducted into the Classification, initiating a new year’s worth of commentary on what is happening in the world of Australian wine.”

 

‘2026 Classification ranks and movers’

The 2026 collection features 76 Three Merit wines, 234 Two Merit wines and 354 One Merit wines.

Four wines achieved the required 10-vintage review benchmark this year and shot straight into Three Merit status:

  • Hentley Farm Clos Otto Shiraz (Barossa Valley, SA)
  • Chatto Isle Pinot Noir (Tasmania, TAS)
  • Vasse Felix Tom Cullity Cabernet Sauvignon Malbec (Margaret River, WA)
  • Gralyn Artizan Rare Muscat (Margaret River, WA)

Five wines were elevated from Two Merits to Three Merits following high-scoring reviews in the past year:

  • Yarra Yering Dry Red Wine No. 1 (Yarra Valley, VIC)
  • House of Arras Grand Vintage (Tasmania, TAS)
  • Savaterre Chardonnay (Beechworth, VIC)
  • De Bortoli Noble One (Riverina, NSW)
  • Crawford River Riesling (Henty, VIC)

 

‘Emerging trends in the 2026 update’

The Real Review said that, while highlighting Australia’s classic varietal icons, the development of the Classification program has seen an emergence of alternative varieties gaining placement in the One and Two Merit rankings.

“It is gratifying to see a diversity of grape varieties represented in the Classification. This has widened and we expect it to widen further as years pass and more outstanding wines are made from fringe varieties, which are accumulating more vintages and approaching the 10-vintage minimum. This year we see varieties like Nebbiolo, Nero D’Avola, Sangiovese, and a bounty of Grenache among the new One and Two Merit wines,” said Hooke.

“It’s exciting to watch this project evolve, and we take this opportunity to congratulate the producers of all classified wines on their excellent work.”

content:
NSW Wine said the event will return this November after two successful years. Image supplied

NSW Wine has announced the return of NSW Wine Month this November, with “more events, more participating wineries and more venues across the state putting the focus squarely on the best local wines, and the people behind them”.

Formally kicking off the month-long celebration is the 2026 ICC Sydney NSW Wine Awards on 30 October, where the top honours and trophies will be handed out for the years’ best drops. After that, NSW Wine said it’s 30 days of events, promotions, dinners and celebrations that wine lovers everywhere are invited to join.

Since its conception in 2024, NSW Wine Month “has grown into a far-reaching showcase of the wine regions, varieties and personalities that make NSW the incredible state of wine it is”.

“At its heart NSW Wine Month is about building stronger, lasting connections between our regional farmers and businesses, and consumers across the state,” said Mark Bourne, NSW Wine president.

“The month is packed with unique opportunities to enjoy beautiful wine, hear stories from the 200 years of grape growing and winemaking history in NSW and discover something completely new at our flagship festival Sydney Cellar Door from 13-15 November with more than 35 wineries heading to First Fleet Park in The Rocks.”

Minister for Jobs and Tourism Steve Kamper said the state government is proud to support NSW Wine Month as it enters its third successful year.

“The event will showcase the quality and diversity of our state’s world-class wine regions and vineyards, giving thousands of people an opportunity to meet the award-winning winemakers behind them.

“With tastings, winemaker dinners, masterclasses and other events taking place throughout November, there has never been a better time to discover NSW wine.”

NSW Wine said highlights of the month include:

  • The return of the flagship three-day wine festival ‘Sydney Cellar Door’
  • A first-ever ‘Hunter Valley Heritage Vineyard’ event for trade and consumers, bringing 13 winemakers to Sydney for a tasting and dinner with wines from some of the oldest vineyards
  • 2026 NSW Sommelier Wine List of the Year winner Altitude Restaurant will host Tyrrells, Brokenwood, Ross Hill and Clonakilla for one night only
  • Sit down for winemaker dinners with Margan x Botanica, Rowlee x Bibo, Scarbrough Wine Co. x Annata, See Saw Wine x Whitney’s Restaurant & Bar, Molly Morgan Wines x Signal Box Newcastle, plus many more
  • Events like Zecca Handmade Italian × Via Pola Wines and the three Urban Wine Walks (Balmain, Newtown and Newcastle) will shine a light on young and emerging wineries
  • A one-off new world versus old world tasting showdown at The Art Syndicate
  • The Newcastle East City Cellar Door Tasting Trail will bring together seven of the region’s producers under one roof
  • Featured NSW Wine Lists, winemaker takeovers and tasting flights will pop up at venues across the state, including Argyle Precinct and 8 at Trinity.

NSW Wine said the event will be supported again by The Rocks, ICC Sydney, Destination NSW, Good Food and The WinedUp Podcast.

title: Vineyard management at your fingertips
summary:
For years, Jonathan Hambrook has managed vineyards the same way many growers do: juggling spreadsheets, paper notes, text messages and the constant challenge of keeping track of what needs to be done across the property. But rather than accept the administrative headaches as part of the job, the owner and vigneron of Stockman’s Ridge Wines in Orange decided that something needed to be done to smooth out vineyard operations. The result is VineTrack, a vineyard management app designed to bridge the gap between field work and office operations. Journalist Kyra Trussell spoke with Hambrook about the inspiration behind the new platform and how it aims to help vineyard businesses work smarter, not harder.

The post Vineyard management at your fingertips appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
The new app designed ‘by industry for industry’

For years, Jonathan Hambrook has managed vineyards the same way many growers do: juggling spreadsheets, paper notes, text messages and the constant challenge of keeping track of what needs to be done across the property. But rather than accept the administrative headaches as part of the job, the owner and vigneron of Stockman’s Ridge Wines in Orange decided that something needed to be done to smooth out vineyard operations. The result is VineTrack, a vineyard management app designed to bridge the gap between field work and office operations. Journalist Kyra Trussell spoke with Hambrook about the inspiration behind the new platform and how it aims to help vineyard businesses work smarter, not harder.

Jonathan Hambrook says the idea for the app arose from the “day-to-day reality of running and managing vineyard work”.

“Like many vineyard businesses, we had a lot of information spread across custom Excel spreadsheets, paper records, notebooks, text messages, whiteboards and memory. The spreadsheets were useful for calculations and planning, but they did not bring everything together, and they were not practical to use in the field,” he explained.

Moreover, he shared that field records were often just paper notes written whilst actively driving along rows of vines to check for issues. He knew that this wasn’t feasible, admitting that important details can easily be missed or forgotten during busy seasonal periods.

“A fellow viticulturist also described a vision for a tool where an operator could simply press a button while doing a job to record an issue, so [that] another team could come back later and complete the repair. That idea helped shape the first build, which started with pin drops, spray trip recording and spray program management.”

He highlighted that the app was not made by looking at other platforms and trying to copy them, but by asking, “what do vineyards actually need?”.

“There are general farm-management apps, spray program tools and mapping systems available, but we saw a gap for a vineyard-specific, mobile-first platform backed by a powerful web portal. VineTrack is not just a product that puts geofences around blocks and drops pins at GPS locations…the workflows are built around blocks, rows, spray jobs, vineyard machinery, field observations, trips, fuel, maintenance and the way teams move through a vineyard during the season.

“Pins can be attached to vineyard rows, and duplicate detection is based on linear distance along the row rather than simply raw GPS distance. This means users can record two issues that may be very close together physically, but on separate rows, and still find them later using practical vineyard directions.

“For example, a pin can guide someone to a specific row, side and direction of travel, such as ‘Row 101.5, left-hand side, facing north’. That is much more useful for vineyard teams than a simple GPS point on a map.”

Hambrook’s emphasis on making a program that functioned the way vineyards actually work led to one of the app’s crucial features being developed – its ability to run offline.

“Many vineyards are in regional, hilly or remote locations where mobile coverage can be unreliable, so the system has been designed with that reality in mind.

“Users can continue capturing field-based information while they are out in the vineyard, including trips, work activity, spray records, vineyard observations, pins, machinery use and other operational records. The idea is that staff should be able to record information where the work actually happens, rather than waiting until they are back in the office and relying on memory,” he said.

 

Improving visibility

The vigneron believes the main benefit of the app for vineyard operations is visibility.

“VineTrack helps vineyard businesses see what work has been completed, where it happened, who completed it, what machinery was used and what it cost. That can help reduce missed records, improve spray compliance, support audit preparation, track machinery and fuel use, manage maintenance and build a clearer operational history over time. For owners and managers, that means better information for planning, budgeting and understanding the true cost of vineyard work.

“It also helps turn field observations into actions. For example, if someone sees a broken post, pest pressure, disease symptoms, irrigation issue or hazard, they can record it in the field so it can be reviewed and followed up rather than forgotten.”

He also described how the app helps to reduce repetition and manual administration, with tasks and data entry being hosted in one place for everyone in the vineyard to access.

“We are continuing to build this area further as more vineyard businesses approach us with their needs and ideas,” he added.

The development of the app wasn’t without its teething problems, however, with Hambrook noting that building software for vineyards is “very different” from building a simple office-based system.

“The app has to work around real field conditions, patchy reception, GPS accuracy, different block layouts, row detection, machinery workflows, spray records, weather data, and the need for information to sync between mobile devices and the office portal.

“One of the biggest challenges has been making the system powerful enough to capture meaningful vineyard information, but still simple enough to use during a busy workday. If it is too complicated, people will not use it in the field.

“There have also been technical challenges around row detection, syncing data, supporting offline workflows, connecting the app and portal, and making sure records are structured in a way that is useful for compliance, reporting and future decision-making.

“The development process has been very practical. We keep testing it against real vineyard situations and asking whether it would actually help someone on a tractor, in the shed or managing the business from the office. That has shaped the platform from the beginning,” he affirmed.

Early feedback for the app has been positive, says Hambrook, particularly around the need for a tool that reflects how vineyard work happens.

“We are very open to ideas from industry colleagues and have taken their recommendations on board as we continue to streamline the tool for in-field use.

“There has also been strong interest in the low-reception capability, spray records, field observations, machinery and fuel tracking and the ability for a manager in the office to see what has been recorded from the field.

“A lot of the feedback has reinforced the same theme: vineyard businesses do not just need more data, they need practical information they can trust and use.”

The app is free for users to download and use for three months, moving to a subscription model after the trial period has elapsed.

“The subscription model allows us to continue improving the product, supporting users, maintaining the cloud systems behind it and adding new features as vineyard businesses need them.

“The goal is to keep pricing practical for growers and vineyard businesses, while still providing a professional tool that can support field records, spray compliance, machinery, fuel, maintenance, reporting and team-based vineyard management. There is pricing designed for sole operators through to larger vineyard businesses and enterprises,” Hambrook explained.

The app is currently available for Apple devices; however, the web-based portal can be accessed simply by using a browser.

Hambrook remarked that the focus for him has been on getting the Apple version working well first, with an Android version currently in development and expected to launch in the coming months.

summary:

Coal Pit owner Rosie Dunphy said the appointment formally recognises the role Willner has naturally grown into since joining the company. “This appointment feels less like a change and more like recognising the leadership Anika has already shown. The post Coal Pit appoints long-standing winemaker to general manager position appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
Anika Willner joined the winery back in 2018 and has now been appointed as general manager. Image supplied

Coal Pit winery in Central Otago, New Zealand, has appointed its long-standing winemaker Anika Willner to the position of general manager.

Willner will continue her duties as winemaker, “bringing the vineyard, winery and wider business together under her leadership”.

Since joining Coal Pit in 2018, the winery said she has guided the development of its wines, deepened its commitment to organic farming and helped shape the business into “the distinctive Central Otago producer it is today”.

Coal Pit owner Rosie Dunphy said the appointment formally recognises the role Willner has naturally grown into since joining the company.

“Anika knows every aspect of Coal Pit from the ground up. She has cared for this vineyard and shaped its wines with extraordinary energy, commitment and vision. She understands what makes Coal Pit special: the beauty and precision of this site, and the potential of its soils. Combined with her drive and attention to detail, that understanding continues to guide wines of the highest quality and character,” said Dunphy.

“This appointment feels less like a change and more like recognising the leadership Anika has already shown. I am incredibly proud of what she has achieved and delighted to have her leading Coal Pit into its next chapter.”

Her appointment comes at an “important stage” for Coal Pit, following continued investment in the vineyard and winery, the development of its Central Otago single-vineyard programme and the establishment of Chardonnay on the Gibbston property.

“Coal Pit has been my home for much of my winemaking life. I have grown alongside this vineyard, and I feel a real sense of responsibility to care for what has been built here while continuing to ask what it can become,” Willner said.

“There is still so much to learn from this site. I’m excited to bring the vineyard, winery and wider business even closer together and continue building on the potential I know this vineyard has.”

Alongside her work at Coal Pit, Willner is an active contributor to the wider wine industry. She chairs New Zealand’s Organic, Regenerative and Biodynamic Winegrowing Conference and serves as the New Zealand representative for The Porto Protocol, an international wine-industry climate action organisation.

Originally from Ohio, the winery said she “brought extensive international experience to Coal Pit”, having worked across South Africa, Germany, Tasmania, Oregon, Burgundy, California and Marlborough before making Gibbston her home.
